entry.independence_analysis: The 1845 baptism (a_018) is a primary parish record that states the father's name at the event, and it is independent of the census-based assertions (a_004, a_005), which are inferred from household position and shared surname. The I2 side rests on two census entries (1850, 1860) that depend on the same household and the same unknown informant, so they count as one body of evidence for identity, not two. The I3 side rests on the 1840 Luzerne census (a_014, a_015) and the 1840 county death record (a_016), which are independent of the baptism. Note: the tool's conflicts_surfaced entry cites a_004 as coming from S2 and S3; the assertion a_004 is actually drawn from S1 (src_001, the 1850 census). The S2 and S3 records are the 1860 census and the death certificate, whose father-related assertions are a_013 (death certificate, son-in-law informant) and the 1860 relationship a_010. This does not change the analysis but should be corrected in the tree-side link.
entry.weighing_analysis: Decisive factor one: the death record (a_016, primary, county clerk, confident link in pe_008) states that the Luzerne Thomas Flynn died 15 September 1840, nearly five years before the baptism of 3 August 1845. A dead man cannot be the father named at a 1845 baptism, so the I3 link to a_018 is excluded unless the 1840 death record is of a different Thomas, which the evidence does not show. Decisive factor two: the I2 candidate has no positive tie to the baptism. Its evidence is a Schuylkill census household (1850 and 1860) and a 1842 Philadelphia marriage whose age (19) conflicts with the census-implied birth year (~1818), a 5-year gap. The baptism place (Luzerne) is roughly 50 miles from the Schuylkill household, so I2 being in Luzerne in 1845 is possible but unproven. The baptism itself is strong evidence that a Thomas Flynn was the father; the open question is which Thomas.
entry.resolution_rationale: The problem: the tree cannot attach the 1845 baptized child to a Thomas Flynn until it is known which man is meant, because the two candidates would give Patrick different fathers and different family histories. The evidence: the baptism (a_018) names a Thomas Flynn as father, a primary record made at the event. The Luzerne Thomas Flynn (I3) is shown dead in 1840 (a_016), so the I3 link is rejected as an identity match for the 1845 father, and the link recorded at pe_010 (speculative) should be withdrawn. Which version is more reliable: the I3 candidate is excluded on a primary death record, which is the strongest rationale available (rationale 3, substantially less credible given the impossibility). But excluding I3 does not establish I2, and no assertion positively places the Schuylkill Thomas in Luzerne County in 1845, so there is no preferred assertion and the conflict cannot be resolved as stated. Why the error exists: the baptism clerk or the parish record likely named a Thomas Flynn from the Luzerne community without distinguishing between same-name men, a common pattern when two unrelated men of one name live in neighbouring counties; alternatively, the parish entry predates a later clarification. Decisive records that would settle it: the full 1845 baptism entry (the child's name, sponsors, and parents' residence, to tie the baptism to Patrick); Luzerne County and Wilkes-Barre records from 1841-1850 naming Thomas Flynn with a residence; Schuylkill County records from 1843-1848 (Pottsville or St. Clair parish baptisms, marriage register, land or tax lists) placing the Schuylkill Thomas in one place; and the 1842 Philadelphia marriage record for the wife's residence. A conclusion that Patrick's father is Thomas Flynn cannot be proved until the identity question is resolved.
